title: THE WORLD'S RICHEST INVESTORS USE THESE TINY ISLANDS. HERE'S WHY

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: Your retirement money could be passing through a tiny island in the Caribbean right now.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: You've probably never been there. You might not even know where it is on a map.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: But some of the world's largest investment funds are legally registered there.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: Funds connected to wealthy investors, major financial institutions, and retirement savings.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: And here's the strange part. The money doesn't necessarily stay on the island.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: It might never physically go there at all.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: So why would an investment company in New York set up a fund thousands of miles away on a Caribbean island?

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: By the third quarter of 2026, more than 31,500 regulated investment funds were registered in the Cayman Islands.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: On three small islands in the Caribbean Sea.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: These aren't all small private accounts belonging to people trying to hide money.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: And the deeper you follow the money, the stranger the picture becomes.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: Look at the western Caribbean.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: South of Cuba and northwest of Jamaica, you'll find three islands.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: Together, they form the Cayman Islands, a British Overseas Territory.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: For much of its history, Cayman was a small maritime community. People made their living through fishing, seafaring, and trade.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: There was no enormous manufacturing industry. No vast domestic market. No major stock exchange.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: According to historical records, the first commercial bank opened in 1953. Barclays established a presence in George Town.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: Think about what that means. When New York and London had already spent generations building powerful banking institutions, Cayman was only beginning.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: In 1970, Cayman's recorded population was only 10,249.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: But while Cayman's domestic economy was small, the international financial system was changing.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: After the Second World War, international commerce expanded. Multinational companies became more important.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: US dollars were increasingly being deposited, borrowed, and lent through financial institutions outside the United States. This became known as the Eurodollar market.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: And this is where Cayman's story takes an unexpected turn. Its leaders began building an industry around something that couldn't be mined, shipped, or manufactured.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: They built it around law.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: In 1966, new legislation was introduced to encourage the banking industry. Company law, trust arrangements, and professional services developed alongside.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: There was another attraction. Cayman did not impose the kind of ordinary direct income taxes found in many larger economies.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: But if low taxes alone created successful financial centers, every jurisdiction with low taxes would become a global financial powerhouse. That hasn't happened.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: Investors also care about whether contracts can be enforced. They care about company law, access to legal professionals, accountants, and regulators.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: By the time global investment funds became a much larger industry, Cayman already had part of the necessary infrastructure.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: Imagine you own a business. Its headquarters are in London. Its customers are in America. Its factories are in Vietnam.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: Where is the business? There isn't one answer that describes everything it does.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: A financial company can be legally registered in the Cayman Islands while the people making its investment decisions work in New York.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: This is the first thing you need to understand about offshore finance. A fund can be registered in a country without all its money being deposited there.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: Let's build a hypothetical example. Imagine a pension fund called Northbridge Retirement Fund.

visual.title: NORTHBRIDGE RETIREMENT FUND
visual.sub: Managing retirement savings for thousands of workers

segments.speaker: PENSION_MGR
segments.text: We need to allocate part of our portfolio to an international investment fund.

segments.speaker: LAWYER
segments.text: The fund's managers specialize in businesses across several countries. It's established in the Cayman Islands.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: Northbridge reviews the legal documents. It examines the investment strategy, fees, risks, and reporting. Then it subscribes for an interest.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: The fund buys into a manufacturing company in Germany. Northbridge's economic exposure is now connected, through the fund, to a business operating in Germany.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: The German company grows. Its value rises. The fund sells at a profit. Northbridge receives its share.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: Where did the profit come from? Economically, from the performance of the underlying investment. Where was the vehicle registered? Cayman.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: And that's why the popular idea of money simply being sent away to an island and sitting there misses so much of what is happening.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: Why do investors keep choosing the same places? Why not establish every fund in the country where the manager works?

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: Imagine you're starting an investment fund. You have potential investors in six countries. You need experienced lawyers, administrators, auditors, and reliable rules.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: For many international managers, Cayman falls into the category of a jurisdiction where an established professional industry already understands the type of fund you're creating.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: This is the advantage of specialization. Over time, thousands of funds have been established there. Law firms developed expertise. Administrators became familiar with the procedures.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: By the third quarter of 2026, the regulator recorded 13,187 mutual funds and 18,360 private funds. Together, 31,547 regulated funds.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: There is also the tax treatment. Cayman generally does not impose direct income taxes on investment funds.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: But it's essential to understand what that does and does not mean. It doesn't make the investors automatically tax-free.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: An investor may still owe tax under the laws of their own country. The underlying investment can also generate taxes where business activity takes place.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: In March 2026, the Bank for International Settlements published research on cross-border financial centers.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: By 2023, these centers accounted for almost sixty trillion dollars in external financial positions. Nearly thirty percent of the worldwide total.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: Yet the economies of those same centers represented just 2.8 percent of global economic activity.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: From 1980 to 2023, the share of worldwide external financial positions associated with these centers increased from around twelve percent to nearly thirty percent.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: In November 2026, the United States Treasury published detailed figures showing where American investors held foreign securities at the end of 2025.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: You might expect the largest destination to be Britain. Or Japan. Perhaps Canada, one of America's largest trading partners.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: But the jurisdiction at the top of that particular list wasn't any of them. It was the Cayman Islands.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: American investors held approximately 3.07 trillion dollars in foreign securities attributed to Cayman. More than the two trillion attributed to the United Kingdom.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: Cayman didn't suddenly become a bigger industrial economy than Japan. The figures measure market value of securities held through Cayman-domiciled fund structures.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: If so much of this system is legitimate, why has offshore finance developed such a troubling reputation?

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: The answer begins with the difference between financial privacy and financial secrecy.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: Imagine a person owns a company. That company owns another company. The second owns a third. And the third holds a financial asset.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: Who ultimately controls the asset? This is known as beneficial ownership. And it becomes crucial when investigators are trying to determine whether financial activity is lawful.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: Financial secrecy can help conceal corruption. It can make tax evasion harder to detect. It can be used in money laundering.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: But we need to separate several activities that are often confused. Tax planning is not automatically tax evasion. International investment is not automatically money laundering.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: In 2021, the Financial Action Task Force placed the Cayman Islands under increased monitoring.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: It did not mean every financial business in Cayman was engaged in wrongdoing. It meant the framework for preventing financial crime needed improvements.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: Cayman undertook reforms. In October 2023, FATF announced the Cayman Islands would no longer be subject to its increased monitoring process.

visual.title: FATF
visual.sub: Cayman Islands removed from increased monitoring — October 2023

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: But in June 2026, the OECD published findings on Cayman's implementation of tax information exchange standards. The findings were mixed.

visual.title: OECD REVIEW
visual.sub: Tax Information Exchange — Cayman Islands, June 2026

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: For the monitored period covering 2023 and 2024, Cayman reported that only 23 percent of incoming requests received responses within ninety days.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: This is important because it shows how financial regulation works in the real world. A jurisdiction can strengthen its rules and still face practical problems.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: Cayman belongs to a much wider network. Pull back from the Caribbean.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: Bermuda has developed important insurance and reinsurance businesses. The British Virgin Islands became known for international corporate services.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: Luxembourg and Ireland are major investment fund domiciles within European regulatory frameworks. Jersey and Guernsey have their own traditions of trusts and financial services.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: Could the world simply stop using small offshore financial centers?

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: Suppose a group of major economies decided that investment funds should no longer use Cayman. Some funds might move to other jurisdictions. Some managers might reorganize.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: But the underlying need to organize international investments would not disappear. Investors would still live in different countries. Businesses would still need capital.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: History tells us that centers of financial power do not stay in the same places forever.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: Venice was once an important center of international commerce. Amsterdam became a major financial hub. London expanded its global influence over centuries.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: When you see a major financial position recorded in a small island jurisdiction, you're not necessarily seeing where that wealth was created.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: The world economy isn't connected by roads, ports, and shipping lanes alone. It's also connected by contracts, ownership structures, investment funds, banks, and laws.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: This is Farthing Explains. Explaining how money shapes the world.

segments.speaker: NARRATOR
segments.text: If this documentary changed how you see the global financial system, share it with someone who might find the story surprising.
